meta.description: Not Charles Darwin. This quip appears in none of his writings — it's an anonymous metaphor from the 1840s, later mis-pinned to Darwin (probably via Lord Bowen).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A mathematician is a blind man in a dark room looking for a black cat which isn't there'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Darwin. It's an anonymous 19th-c. saying; the Darwin credit is a modern misattribution the earliest source (1940) already doubted.

answer.label: Not Charles Darwin — an anonymous saying he never wrote
answer.authorDates: Metaphor in print since the 1840s · no author ever identified
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in none of Charles Darwin’s books, letters, or papers, and there is no anecdote of him saying it. Quote Investigator traces the “blind man in a dark room… black cat” metaphor to an 1846 Missouri newspaper, with no famous author attached; the “mathematician…Darwin” pairing surfaces only decades later — and the earliest such citation, in a 1940 mathematics journal, already flagged it as doubtful (“He probably never did”).

source.heading: The record

docMeta.dd: The American Mathematical Monthly, 1940 — and already skeptical

source.excerpt: “A mathematician is a blind man in a dark room looking for a black cat which isn’t there.”
trail: Quote Investigator locates the metaphor in an 1846 Missouri newspaper with no author, and quotes a 1940 American Mathematical Monthly item that already doubted the Darwin credit: “He probably never did.”
The line sits in the Misattributed section of Wikiquote’s Charles Darwin page, which traces the earliest firm versions to the English judge Lord Bowen.
Wikipedia’s Black cat analogy entry lists the Darwin form as a misquotation and dates the saying to “at least the 1890s… its absolute origin is unknown.”
A mathematics quotations page files the exact line as “Unknown (often wrongly attributed to Charles Darwin).”
source.excerptNote: The wording most often circulated online under Darwin’s name. Early printed forms use “black hat” rather than “black cat.”

source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identified author or first-publication source — it is an anonymous 19th-century saying that evolved across many hands. With no attributable work or date, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted; the metaphor’s underlying form is old enough to be in the public domain, but the specific “mathematician…Darwin” wording cannot be tied to any single protectable source.

author.heading: Who was Charles Darwin?
author.metaLine: 1809–1882 · English naturalist, author of On the Origin of Species
author.bio: Charles Robert Darwin was the English naturalist whose On the Origin of Species (1859) established evolution by natural selection. His surviving writings — books, notebooks, and thousands of letters — are among the most exhaustively catalogued of any scientist. That completeness matters here: the quip about the mathematician and the black cat is nowhere in them, and no contemporary ever reported him saying it.

misattribution.heading: Why Darwin gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The Darwin credit is late, thin, and doubted from its first appearance. The metaphor is an anonymous stock joke that drifted across professions (metaphysician, philosopher, theologian, mathematician) and famous names for over a century.

items.why: The line is in none of Darwin’s books, letters, or notebooks, and no contemporary reports it. Its earliest link to Darwin — a 1940 American Mathematical Monthly note — itself hedged: “I have heard it said that Charles Darwin gave the following. (He probably never did.)”

The English judge Charles Bowen’s earliest attested form — an 1894 Pall Mall Gazette item — is the “blind man…black hat” quip; the “metaphysician…black hat” framing credited to Bowen surfaces only later (an 1906 Fortnightly Review item). The near-rhyme of metaphysician / mathematician and Bowen / Darwin is a plausible route by which the credit slid onto Darwin — an observation, not a proven chain.

items.who: William James, Lord Balfour, H. L. Mencken
items.why: Per Wikiquote and Quote Investigator, the same metaphor has been pinned to several figures with small wording changes — a hallmark of a floating anonymous saying, not a sourced quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: an anonymous 19th-century metaphor of unknown origin — Darwin almost certainly never said or wrote it.

context.heading: A joke that changes jobs
lead: The gag works by swapping one profession for another. Lord Bowen’s metaphysician gropes in a dark room for a black hat that isn’t there; William James applied it to the philosopher; a later punchline adds a theologian who “finds the cat.” The mathematician version — the one now glued to Darwin online — is just another substitution in a long-running template.

That fluidity is the tell. Genuine quotations have a fixed source; floating jokes accrete famous names to sound weightier. By the time the internet made Darwin the default author, the saying was already roughly a century old and had never had one.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator tracks a companion “philosopher / theologian” version whose punchline — the theologian triumphantly announces he has found the cat — appears with Lewis Browne (1931), Eric Temple Bell (1934), Julian Huxley (by 1939), and H. L. Mencken (1942).
None of these forms cites Darwin, and the mathematician-plus-Darwin pairing remains the youngest and least supported branch of the family.
context.pull: Genuine quotations have a source. Floating jokes collect famous names instead.
